stories.topic: The Bank That Wanted to Put a Five Star in Its ATM
stories.summary: Many years ago, a bank wanted to encourage retail customers to use ATMs instead of branch counters. They had the idea of stocking the ATM with Cadbury 5 Star chocolates so that any withdrawal above Rs 5,000 would also dispense a candy. They had to seek the regulator's approval. The regulator denied permission, ruling that it was 'undignified' to dispense a candy bar alongside cash.
stories.insight: A perfect cameo of intrusive central planning by regulators. Product and process decisions that should be the birthright of a firm are surrendered to a feudal lord whose taste-driven veto kills innovation. When everything is banned by default and you must come asking for permission, regulation has stopped correcting market failure and become petty rule by whim.

stories.topic: The Only Job Interview of His Life — for FSLRC
stories.summary: When the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission was being set up under Justice Sri Krishna in 2011, Ajay was made to face the only job interview of his entire life — interviewed by the judge himself for a place on the technical team. He came out of it co-leading the research team (with Ila Patnaik) that supported a four-year, two-volume rewrite of Indian financial law.
stories.insight: A small biographical detail that quietly underlines how Indian public-policy careers actually work — not through annual hiring rounds and CVs, but through being known and trusted by a few people doing serious work. The intellectual ecosystem is thin enough that the gatekeeper for a once-in-a-generation reform project is one chair, one room, one conversation.

stories.topic: M.S. Sahu Did Separation of Powers Inside His Own Regulator
stories.summary: M.S. Sahu — among the first to publicly diagnose the violation of separation of powers in Indian regulators — became the first chairman of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India. The IBC's draft had originally imported FSLRC's 140 checks-and-balances sections, but those were stripped out when it went into government and the bad SEBI Act sections were imported instead. As chairman, Sahu split IBBI internally into legislative, executive, and judicial departments, and the IBBI board enacted a regulation governing how IBBI makes regulations — even though the parent law did not require it.
stories.insight: When you can't fix the law, you can sometimes still fix the practice. A reformer who knew the theory used the discretionary power he was given to bind himself, importing checks and balances voluntarily. It's a model for how you make progress in a system where the cathedral never gets built — you smuggle the architecture in section by section.

stories.topic: Three Regulators Now Govern How They Make Regulations
stories.summary: After Sahu's IBBI experiment slumbered for some years, SEBI recently came out with its own regulation governing how SEBI makes regulations, importing the FSLRC bag of ideas. On the morning of recording, Ajay got an SMS that the RBI had done the same. So as of May 2025, three Indian regulatory organisations have boards that have approved meta-regulations binding their own regulation-making.
stories.insight: A 25-year intellectual journey from 'who even thinks about this?' to 'no one in good faith can argue for unchecked regulatory power' — won not by a single big-bang law but by repeated, patient persuasion until the practitioners themselves chose to import the ideas. The intellectual argument is won; the implementation will take another decade.

stories.topic: David Stockman, Bitter in Mid-1980s Washington
stories.summary: Jonathan Rauch in Government's End recounts meeting David Stockman, Reagan's man and the budget director who was supposed to deliver the small-government revolution. Even as 'the president's man', Stockman was depressed and bitter, telling Rauch how impossible it had become to actually get anything reformed in DC. Both Bill Clinton and Newt Gingrich later tried in their own ways and failed.
stories.insight: Demosclerosis is not a partisan complaint — it defeats reformers of every stripe because it is structural. Once interest groups multiply and concentrated benefits with diffuse costs are entrenched, even a reformist president's chief of budget can't move the machine. The lesson for India: don't wait until you reach the American level of regulatory ossification.

stories.summary: When the Shah Rukh Khan film Raees came out, Amit wrote about how it got the basic economics wrong. The film had a politician campaigning for prohibition while Shah Rukh's bootlegger character tried to stop him. In reality, the Baptist (the moralising politician) and the bootlegger are natural allies — the bootlegger's whole business depends on prohibition. He should have been funding the politician's campaign, not opposing him.
stories.insight: A pop-culture beat for Bruce Yandle's 'Bootleggers and Baptists.' The mechanism of regulation is rarely a clean fight between virtue and vice — moral entrepreneurs and the entrenched profit-takers usually want the same outcome for opposite reasons. Spotting a 'Baptist' campaigning for a ban should make you ask: who is the bootlegger funding this?

stories.topic: Donald Trump Did What Indian Reformers Could Not
stories.summary: Indian economists and policy thinkers spent decades arguing that India's tariffs should come down. None of them got the job done. Then Donald Trump's tariff brinksmanship pushed India into signing a free trade agreement with the UK with a ten-year glide path to zero tariffs on 80% of products and government procurement opened to UK firms. Ajay's deadpan reaction: 'You and I should nominate Donald Trump for the Bharat Ratna.'
stories.insight: Reform doesn't always travel the road you expected. The intellectual case is necessary, but a sudden external shock can do in months what decades of careful argument couldn't. The honest reformer's job is to keep the ideas ready in the cupboard — so that when the political weather shifts, the better policy is the one that gets pulled out.

recommendations.creator: Susan Dudley and Jerry Brito
recommendations.context: A book on the working of regulation, mostly with an American focus.
recommendations.reason: The first and last chapters are relevant to the general theory of regulation. Most of the book is about how regulation works in America, but it covers a useful sample of the territory mapped in the episode.

recommendations.item: Government's End: Why Washington Stopped Working
recommendations.creator: Jonathan Rauch
recommendations.context: Rauch's book that introduced the term demosclerosis.
recommendations.reason: Blew Amit's mind when he first read it. Lays out how interest groups multiply, regulations grow, and reform becomes structurally impossible — with the David Stockman and Clinton/Gingrich vignettes that show even presidents can't move the machine.

recommendations.creator: George Stigler
recommendations.context: Stigler's 1971 essay laying out three axioms of regulatory capture.
recommendations.reason: The intellectual foundation for taking the public-interest theory of regulation seriously and then moving past it: the state has coercive power, private parties benefit by directing it, so it is in everyone's rational self-interest to capture it. Once you absorb this you can't unsee it.

recommendations.item: Bootleggers and Baptists — The Education of a Regulatory Economist
recommendations.creator: Bruce Yandle
recommendations.context: Yandle's classic essay on how moralisers and profiteers end up on the same side of regulation.
recommendations.reason: Beautiful and durable frame for thinking about how regulation actually gets enacted. The moral campaigner provides the public legitimacy; the rent-seeker provides the funding; both want the same ban — for opposite reasons.

recommendations.item: Fortress and Frontier in American Health Care
recommendations.creator: Robert Graboyes
recommendations.context: Graboyes' book contrasting fortress (regulated healthcare) with frontier (open tech).
recommendations.reason: Won the Bastiat Prize in 2014. Introduced Amit to the fortress-and-frontier framework — heavy regulation creates walled industries that block innovation, while permissionless tech becomes the place where breakthroughs happen. Even when regulation seems to address asymmetric information, the lives lost by delay can outweigh the lives saved.

recommendations.item: Raees: An Empty Shell of a Gangster Film
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's review-essay on the Shah Rukh Khan film Raees.
recommendations.reason: The article where Amit calls out the film for getting the economics of bootlegging backwards — the bootlegger should be lobbying for prohibition, not against it. A pop-culture entry into Bootleggers and Baptists.

recommendations.item: The Baptist, the Bootlegger and the Dead Man Walking
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on Yandle's framework.
recommendations.reason: The longer treatment of how regulatory coalitions actually form in India and elsewhere — the moraliser and the rent-seeker walking arm in arm.

recommendations.item: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission Report — Volume 1
recommendations.creator: FSLRC, chaired by Justice B.N. Srikrishna
recommendations.context: The 2013 conceptual volume from FSLRC.
recommendations.reason: A crisp summary of 20 years of research on regulation and regulatory theory in India. Compact chapters explain the thinking on each issue and end with a box of drafting instructions handed to the law team. Ajay calls it the model for how reform documents should be written.

recommendations.item: Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission Report — Volume 2 (Indian Financial Code)
recommendations.creator: FSLRC, chaired by Justice B.N. Srikrishna
recommendations.context: The draft Indian Financial Code.
recommendations.reason: About 140 sections of horizontal regulatory theory plus the financial-system-wide draft law. Ajay says without exaggeration that India has not had a better law-drafting team since independence — the cleanest, most modern law-drafting project in Indian history, a role model for how laws should be drafted.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and colleagues
recommendations.context: The LEAP blog where much of the regulatory-theory literature was developed.
recommendations.reason: Through the 2000s, hundreds of blog articles and dozens of working papers at NIPFP, IGIDR and on the LEAP blog built the Indian literature on what was going wrong under Indian conditions. The body of knowledge that sits behind FSLRC.

recommendations.item: Making Regulation in India Work Better
recommendations.creator: K.P. Krishnan
recommendations.context: Krishnan's lecture on regulatory reform in India.
recommendations.reason: The senior civil servant who launched the FSLRC project from inside the Department of Economic Affairs explains the practitioner's view of why the regulatory state went wrong and how to fix it.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's lecture and slides on Indian regulatory theory.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's own talk that systematises the masterclass given in this episode — separation of powers, rule of law, surgical delegation, checks and balances — with the slides as a companion document.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's Substack post on the current opportunity for deregulation.
recommendations.reason: The longer-form companion to Ajay's argument in the episode — why this is the moment to move on the regulatory-theory agenda, what to demand, and how to think about sequencing.

recommendations.creator: United States Congress
recommendations.context: The 1946 American general law governing federal regulatory agencies.
recommendations.reason: Held up as the kind of horizontal, cross-agency regulatory law India never had. Republican pushback against the proliferation of New Deal agencies; locks in separation of powers, checks and balances, and rule-of-law procedures generally rather than agency by agency.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on what the state is for.
recommendations.reason: The starting point for this episode's argument: the state exists to protect rights, and the rule of law is the umbrella under which markets can work. Required reading before the regulation conversation.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on the four kinds of market failure.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's masterclass on the four market failures that may permit state intervention. The episode that establishes which kinds of market failure can even justify a regulator.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on prohibition and victimless crimes.
recommendations.reason: Bans don't make demand disappear; they create black markets and bootleggers. The downstream proof of why the Bootleggers-and-Baptists frame is not just clever but predictive.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on diabetes and dietary advice.
recommendations.reason: The episode that recounts how the sugar lobby in the 1950s-80s funded fraudulent studies blaming fat instead of sugar — a vivid case of a real-world Bootleggers-and-Baptists capture of dietary regulation.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on public choice theory.
recommendations.reason: Governments are made of people responding to incentives. Bureaucrats want bigger budgets; politicians want re-election. The episode that establishes why government failure is ubiquitous, even when the rhetoric is benevolent.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on innovation and R&D policy.
recommendations.reason: The reference for why a positive-externality problem like R&D calls for vouchers and not for a regulator. The classification of which market failures call for which kinds of state intervention.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's deep dive on separation of powers.
recommendations.reason: The companion episode that lays out why fusing legislative, executive and judicial power inside a regulator is a violation of the basic structure of the constitution — and the recent American developments (right to a jury trial, Chevron) that are pushing back.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on the theory of change.
recommendations.reason: The framework Ajay invokes when talking about why FSLRC didn't fail just because no parliament enacted it. Progress in democracies isn't a cathedral; it's intellectual persuasion over decades, with ideas creeping into practice one by one.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on India's inflation-targeting framework.
recommendations.reason: The proof-of-concept for the FSLRC theory of change — inflation targeting was incubated inside the Indian Financial Code and emerged years later as a separate, working law. Ideas creep into practice.

recommendations.item: India's Massive Pensions Crisis (Episode 347, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive on the new pension scheme.
recommendations.reason: The cautionary case study referenced in this episode: a small intellectual community built and shipped the new pension scheme; when that group dispersed, institutional memory collapsed and the policy was rolled back. Why the ecosystem of ideas-people matters as much as the ideas.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code.
recommendations.reason: The episode that tells the story of how the IBC's draft originally imported FSLRC's 140 checks-and-balances sections, then had them stripped out inside the government and replaced with the bad SEBI Act sections — context for the IBBI vignette.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's first of two episodes on globalisation.
recommendations.reason: Sets up the second piece of good news of this episode — that Ajay's optimistic reading at the close of the globalisation arc is starting to come true with the India-UK FTA.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's second globalisation episode.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Ajay ends with a contrarian, cautiously hopeful reading — exactly the call he is now seeing vindicated by the FTA.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: The standing reference for everything in this episode — public goods vs externalities vs market power, when the state should and shouldn't intervene, and the scaffolding of regulatory theory under Indian conditions.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit and Ajay's online course.
recommendations.reason: The course they have just launched, plugged at the top of the show notes — drawing on the same intellectual territory the show covers.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's writing course.
recommendations.reason: Amit's standing course recommendation — the writing discipline that informs his prose.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Substack newsletter.
recommendations.reason: Amit's standing newsletter — running commentary in the same idiom as the show.

core_ideas.concept: Rule of Law vs Regulation Are Different Things
core_ideas.explanation: People conflate these. Rule of law is the foundational umbrella — everyone knows the law, the law applies equally, there is due process, the prosecutor is not the judge, the law is predictable across time. Markets work beautifully when rule of law is well enforced; competition is the best regulation, because rivalry to serve customers keeps everyone honest. Regulation is something narrower and rarer — state coercion of firms, sometimes justified when a real market failure can't be sorted out by competition under the rule of law.

core_ideas.concept: Only Some Market Failures Justify a Regulator
core_ideas.explanation: Of the four canonical market failures, only two-and-a-half can possibly justify a regulator. Public goods are best handled by the government making or buying them. Positive externalities call for vouchers. Negative externalities, asymmetric information, and market power may justify regulation. Even there, a market failure is necessary but not sufficient — most of the time the right answer is to do nothing, because government failure is ubiquitous and the cure can be worse than the disease.

Regulation is the business of state coercion oriented towards firms. Regulators are specialised arms of the state that do regulation; you can also do regulation through a normal government department. Regulatory theory is the general, horizontal technology — separation of powers, rule of law procedures, checks and balances, surgical delegation — that applies across airports, banks, drugs, securities. Domain knowledge sits on top of that foundation, not in place of it.
core_ideas.quote: Regulators only do regulation, but not all regulation is done by regulators.

core_ideas.concept: Capture, Stigler's Three Axioms, Concentrated Benefits and Diffuse Costs
core_ideas.explanation: Stigler's 1971 essay: the state has coercive power; private parties who get the state to use that power for their own ends benefit; therefore it is rational self-interest for every private party to capture the state. The mechanism is concentrated benefits and diffuse costs — a regulation that takes one rupee from each Indian is invisible to each individual but transformative for the firm that captures it. Multiply this by tens of thousands of regulations and you get demosclerosis.
core_ideas.quote: Every regulation harms the people. But the cost is so small in individual terms, and so invisible — the unseen as it were — that we don't even notice and we don't protest.

core_ideas.explanation: Bruce Yandle's framing: regulatory coalitions usually have two faces. The Baptist provides moral legitimacy ('drinking is immoral, ban it'). The bootlegger provides funding, because the ban creates the rents he depends on. They lobby together for the same regulation for opposite reasons — and Bollywood films like Raees, where the bootlegger fights prohibition, get the economics backwards. Modern examples: tobacco companies supporting FDA pre-regulation of new cigarettes (entry barriers), the sugar lobby funding fraudulent studies blaming fat.

core_ideas.concept: Government Failure Is Ubiquitous; Market Failure Is Rare
core_ideas.explanation: The fundamental insight from public choice. Governments are made of people, who respond to incentives — bureaucrats expand budgets, politicians chase re-election. They are not omniscient. So while textbooks emphasise rare market failure, the real world is full of routine government failure. The unseen cost of FDA caution is the lives lost during seven-to-eight-year approval delays. The math of weighing lives saved against lives lost is rarely done.

From Hayek and Mises. Regulation rarely solves the problem it was introduced for; it creates downstream problems that demand more regulation. Rent control causes shortages, which calls for housing subsidies, which calls for zoning laws, which calls for further intervention. The price system, when allowed to work under a strong rule of law, needs very little supplementing. Each new layer of regulation lowers the chance the next one is even necessary.

core_ideas.concept: Why Regulators Were Invented (And Why It's Awkward)
core_ideas.explanation: Two real reasons. One: a government department transfers people every five years, so domain knowledge is shallow; a regulator can develop specialisation. Two — bigger — regulators were created to deliberately fuse the legislative and executive functions, on the theory that fast-moving fields like securities markets need specialised technical bodies that can write rules and police them. This is a chosen breach of separation of powers, justified only if the breach is surgically narrow: each rule-making power must be a precise delegation, not a feudal grant.
core_ideas.quote: It's like the police and the parliament have been fused into one agency.

core_ideas.explanation: RBI, SEBI and others didn't stop at fusing legislative and executive. They also absorbed the judicial function — the power to award punishments without due process, often without transparency about who is being punished. That is a 17th-century-philosophy monster: legislative, executive, and judicial powers in the same hands, with low rule of law on top. The result is that regulated firms become silent; freedom of speech inside the industry collapses; the regulator becomes a feudal lord and central planning is reborn at finer-grained intrusiveness than the License Raj.
core_ideas.quote: Now you've got a small little world where there is a regulator and there is an industry that is controlled by the regulator. It is complete absolute power.

core_ideas.concept: Liberalisation Did Not Kill Central Planning
core_ideas.explanation: A common but wrong reading of 1991: that we got a great decline of central planning. In fact, about 75% of the economy passed into the footprint of regulators with hundreds of staff conducting more detailed, more intrusive central planning than the pre-1991 state could. Earlier, the state was far away, and ground reality often had room. After regulator proliferation, products and processes inside firms became surveilled and approved. A regulator that 'introduces a product' should make you see red — products should come from firms.
core_ideas.quote: Earlier the Indian state was far away, and in your ground-level reality, you could do whatever you wanted. That changed.

core_ideas.concept: How to Fix It — Surgical Delegation, Process, Checks and Balances
core_ideas.explanation: Narrow down regulation-writing power: each section of the parent law should specify the objective, the balancing considerations, and the limits within which the regulator may write rules. Wrap legislative and executive functions with rule-of-law procedures — published drafts, public consultation, cost-benefit analysis, appealable licensing decisions. Move the judicial function out of the regulator entirely; let the high courts do it, the way Australia and the UK do. The site of action is the drafting of the parent law that creates the regulator.

Unelected officials writing law is uncomfortable in a democracy. The reply is procedural: a regulation should be born from an articulated objective, a published draft, six alternative ways of solving the same problem, a cost-benefit analysis, 90 days of public comment, a research-and-reform community that can criticise it credibly, and a board with a majority of independent (non-civil-servant) directors who must approve it. That ladder of process is what gives an unelected regulator democratic legitimacy.

core_ideas.concept: FSLRC and a Two-Volume Indian Regulatory Theory
core_ideas.explanation: The Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission (2011-2015) under Justice B.N. Srikrishna produced a 140-section horizontal regulatory theory plus a draft Indian Financial Code. Volume 1 is the conceptual document — 20 years of research as elegant chapters ending in drafting instructions. Volume 2 is the cleanest, most modern draft law since independence. The parent law has not been enacted, but pieces have crept into practice — inflation targeting, IBBI's internal separation of powers, and now SEBI's and RBI's meta-regulations on how they make regulations.
core_ideas.quote: The cleanest, well-drafted, modern quality law drafting project that has been done in Indian history.

core_ideas.concept: The Theory of Change Is Persuasion, Not Cathedrals
core_ideas.explanation: There is no single big-bang law that suddenly fixes everything. Progress in a democracy is intellectual persuasion: build a body of knowledge, publish, debate, persuade, and over decades the ideas creep into practice. FSLRC was not enacted, but inflation targeting, monetary policy committee design, and the regulator-on-itself meta-regulations all flowed from it. May 2025 — when RBI joined SEBI and IBBI in self-binding rule-making — is presented as the moment the intellectual argument has been won.

core_ideas.concept: A Country Can Only Be as Good as Its Thinkers
core_ideas.explanation: India's regulators were drafted by well-meaning people who simply did not have the political-philosophy, public-administration, and legal knowledge to do it right. Lawyers in India know how to litigate sections — they don't know how to design them. Designing law is public administration, political philosophy, public economics, history. India's underinvestment in humanities — serious law schools, philosophy departments, political science, public administration — has been very costly. The site of action to become a great country is to build intellectual power.
core_ideas.quote: A country can only be as good as its thinkers.

core_ideas.explanation: The complement to the ecosystem of ideas: an ecosystem of ideas-people. Wherever a research-and-reform community has had staying power on a subject, India has eventually made progress. When the small group disperses (the new pension scheme is the example), institutional memory dies and reforms can be rolled back because no one is left to defend them in public. The future of Indian public policy rides on creating and sustaining these communities — not on staffing today's joint secretary.

core_ideas.concept: Public Policy Requires Expertise, Not Staffing
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's combative position: if you don't have expertise, you have no business being in public policy. Sending college-educated English-speakers to be junior staff to today's joint secretary isn't progress — it's HR for the bureaucracy. Real progress comes from upstream actors who know a subject five, ten, twenty years deeper than the secretary, who can debate and criticise in the public domain, and who are still around when the political weather shifts.
core_ideas.quote: If you don't have expertise, you have no right to have any engagement with public policy.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's intro: 'We have two pieces of good news for you, which are that I'm Amit and he's Ajay.'
Ajay: 'Amitbai, you and I should nominate Donald Trump for the Bharat Ratna.' Amit immediately: 'He's joking. People are gonna clip this and put this on Twitter and say he's a Trump bhakt.'
Amit's blockbuster movie pitch — 'Return to Zero': India invented zero, the foreigners are now bringing zero (tariffs) back to India.
Amit on Ajay's careful pronunciation of 'regulation' and 'regulator': 'I love the way you say regulation and regulator. I could listen to you all day.'
The DC joke from a friend of Amit's: 'You throw a stone in one direction, you'll hit a legal firm; you throw a stone in another direction, you'll hit a lobbying firm.'

Ajay on the candy-bar-in-an-ATM episode: the regulator denied permission because dispensing a candy with cash was 'undignified'. Amit's reaction to the whole regulatory horror story: 'I I I need I need I need to recover.'

Amit on Ajay's recommendations habit: 'Every episode he does this. The sevens are multiplying. Compound interest.' (After Ajay promised seven recommendations next episode, having delivered none this time.)

The closing reveal: Amit's recommended book lives in his loo. Amit's reply: 'You must have sneaked into my loo at my home in Andheri at some point in time. Please do not reveal any of the other books you saw there.'
Amit's image of the slow march of reform: 'One baby step at a time, the infant crawls away from the precipice, but it can still hear the laboured breathing of the monster.'
Ajay's hope for virality: 'Twenty-three years later, Everything is Everything will have its first viral video. That is my hope.'
'Demosclerosis' — Jonathan Rauch's coinage for the paralysing accumulation of interest groups and regulations in Washington.
Hayek and Mises and the Austrian school's 'interventionist spiral' — each regulation begets the next.
George Stigler's three axioms of capture (1971) — the state has coercive power; private parties benefit by directing it; therefore everyone has rational self-interest in capturing it.
'Concentrated benefits and diffuse costs' — the public-choice formula for why bad regulations are stable: the winners care intensely, the losers each lose too little to notice.
Bruce Yandle's 'Bootleggers and Baptists' — the Baptist provides the moral cover, the bootlegger provides the funding, and both lobby together for the same ban.
David Stockman, Reagan's budget director, telling Jonathan Rauch in mid-1980s Washington how impossible reform was — even for the president's own man.
Robert Graboyes' 'Fortress and Frontier' — heavy-walled regulated industries vs the open frontier of tech where innovation can flourish.
Justice B.N. Srikrishna chairing FSLRC, with Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah co-leading the technical team — a once-in-a-generation reform-drafting effort.

M.S. Sahu — the first to publicly diagnose the violation of separation of powers in Indian regulators (2012); later first chairman of IBBI, where he split the agency internally into legislative, executive and judicial departments.
The U.S. Administrative Procedures Act of 1946 — a Republican-led general law for all federal agencies, the kind of horizontal regulatory law India never had.

Recent American doctrines invoked: the Supreme Court's revival of jury-trial rights against in-house SEC adjudication, and the overturning of Chevron Doctrine — both reasserting judicial control of regulatory agencies.
